item.title: She Bashed the Government on a Private Call. Then She Was Detained for Months
item.description:
Until recently, Star Sabga spent her days making artisanal cheese and ranting about politics over the phone with her niece.

Ms. Sabga, 69, lived in a luxury seaside apartment in a suburb of Port of Spain, the capital of Trinidad and Tobago. Her niece, Genevievre Hadeed, and her niece’s husband, a bottled-water magnate named Dominic Hadeed, helped cover her costs.

But in June, that peaceful lifestyle was upended when police officers detained the Hadeeds and Ms. Sabga, accusing them of plotting to assassinate the prime minister.

The Hadeeds were held without charges for nearly a month, and Ms. Sabga for more than two months, under Trinidad’s state of emergency, a measure in place almost continuously since 2025 in response to rising violent crime, according to officials. The state of emergency allows authorities to carry out warrantless searches and detain people indefinitely without charges.

The detentions gripped the Caribbean nation, setting off a national debate about the government’s use of surveillance and preventive detention. The saga also exposed racial and political friction surrounding Trinidad’s Middle Eastern-descended minority, to which Ms. Sabga and the Hadeeds belong.

Kamla Persad-Bissessar, the prime minister, did not respond to questions about the cases of Ms. Sabga and the Hadeeds. But she defended the state of emergency, saying to reporters on Thursday, “It is very clear that the crime stats are down.” She added, “Maybe it’s not the best thing to do, but it was very successful.”

Governments around the region have increasingly turned to severe tactics in response to surging rates of violence. In El Salvador, more than 90,000 people have been detained, and nearly 500 have died in state custody, amid a four-year state of emergency, according to Amnesty International. Honduras and Jamaica have also used states of exception, during which certain rights are suspended amid an emergency, to the alarm of human rights groups.

Sandra Pellegrini, the Latin America regional team lead at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, or A.C.L.E.D., a U.S.-based nonprofit organization that monitors conflict and protest data, has studied the use of emergency powers in the region. She said any reductions in crime have often been short-lived and come at the cost of civil liberties.

“Whether you’re a criminal or not, you’re still supposed to be able to access a fair trial,” she said, noting that protesters and government critics have at times become targets under law enforcement agencies with weakened restrictions.

Before his legal saga made headlines, Mr. Hadeed had been known as a critic of the administration. He criticized its tax policies in a public forum in March and objected to the government’s decision to cancel a lease for land his businesses had operated on since 2007. The Hadeeds were also known as prominent members of Trinidad’s Syrian-Lebanese minority group.

The nation is split almost evenly between Afro-Trinidadians, many of whom are descended from enslaved Africans, and Indo-Trinidadians, who trace their roots to indentured workers from India. Many people also have mixed heritage, and several prominent minority groups exist, including the Syrian-Lebanese.

Middle Eastern-descended Trinidadians have historically been associated with the People’s National Movement, currently the country’s main opposition party, and a notable number of successful businesspeople in the country are of Syrian-Lebanese descent, according to Sam Salloum, a Trinidadian businessman who is part of the community.

Politicians in the United National Congress, the governing party, frequently criticize the economic dominance of the Syrian-Lebanese community — often referred to as “the 1 percent” — and accuse them of political corruption and organized crime.

In June, the attorney general, John Jeremie, issued warnings to the ethnic minority during a motion to extend the nation’s state of emergency. He called them a “gang” that had “taken over” the opposition party.

Members of Parliament enthusiastically thumped their desks, punctuating Mr. Jeremie’s remarks.

Mr. Jeremie also confirmed that some Syrian-Lebanese people have had their U.S. visas revoked. He denied his government’s involvement in those decisions, but implied that U.S. intelligence agencies had flagged them for criminal ties. (The Hadeeds’ lawyer confirmed that their visas were among those that were revoked.)

Ms. Sabga read about Mr. Jeremie’s comments in the next day’s newspaper, according to court documents. Angry, she called her niece, Ms. Hadeed, to vent her frustration with how her community was being treated.

Less than two weeks later, just after dawn on June 24, the Hadeeds were startled awake when police officers, some with machine guns, swept into their home, according to affidavits by the Hadeeds. Officers declared they had a search warrant and seized electronic devices, including those of the Hadeeds’ three children.

It was not until Mr. Hadeed was separated from his wife and detained for multiple days that he was given a reason for the arrests: The Hadeeds were accused of plotting to assassinate the prime minister and other government leaders and of fostering ties to transnational crime.

Mr. Hadeed was “numb with shock, disbelief and horror,” he wrote in an affidavit denying the allegations. He later learned that Ms. Sabga, his wife’s aunt, had also been detained.

“The entire community was in shock,” said Mr. Salloum, who knew Ms. Sabga and the Hadeeds. He said the community knew Ms. Sabga primarily for selling shanklish cheese, balls of fermented and strained yogurt covered in seeds and spices.

Mr. Salloum dismissed the idea that Ms. Sabga could be at the center of an assassination plot, saying she wouldn’t even spray a bug. “She gonna cry for the cockroach,” he said.

The Hadeeds and Ms. Sabga denied the accusations. Through their lawyer, they declined interviews.

In an affidavit, Mr. Hadeed said he suffered from medical conditions that were exacerbated in prison. Ms. Sabga and Ms. Hadeed were held in a women’s prison, where they said in affidavits that they were subjected to strip searches and filthy lodgings with no privacy, even to relieve themselves.

In the following weeks, court records revealed that a central piece of evidence in the case was a recording of the June 11 phone call between Ms. Sabga and Ms. Hadeed, which authorities had intercepted. To date, authorities have not explained why they had tapped the call in the first place, saying only in court documents that security agencies were specially trained to monitor “persons of interest.”

Roger Alexander, the homeland security minister, cited 13 written excerpts from Ms. Sabga’s impassioned conversation with her niece. Ms. Sabga used a slur against the prime minister, an Indo-Trinidadian woman, and called her “a target.”

“Somebody’s getting a bullet in their head,” Ms. Sabga had said. “What has to happen for this to cool down is the death of one of her members of Parliament.”

Mr. Alexander, who did not respond to requests for comment, wrote in a court document that those statements were part of “a developing plot or chatter pointing to threats to the life of persons in public life.” He said the authorities had worked with U.S. “partner agencies” and found that the Hadeeds and Ms. Sabga had connections to criminals, to whom they could “communicate deadly intent.”

The U.S. authorities, including the F.B.I., the Drug Enforcement Administration and the International Law Enforcement division of the Department of Justice, did not confirm or deny any criminal investigations involving the Hadeeds or Ms. Sabga.

The intelligence that authorities relied upon to detain the Hadeeds and Ms. Sabga was called into question when a local news outlet posted a leaked recording of the full 15-minute call in July. The recording showed Ms. Sabga had been privately venting her frustrations about what she saw as a political attack on her community, which she insisted was not involved in criminal activity.

The leak sparked intense and wide-ranging reactions.

Many condemned Ms. Sabga’s use of slurs against the prime minister, for which Ms. Sabga expressed regret in an affidavit — though she said her comments had been “wickedly twisted out of context.” Others saw the recording as discrediting the government’s claims of an assassination plot. The call did not involve Mr. Hadeed, raising questions about why the authorities detained him.

After a month in detention, the authorities released the Hadeeds and revoked their detention orders. A video on social media showed Mr. Hadeed returning to his office, hugging and kissing his employees and saying, “I missed you all.”

In July, Ms. Sabga was released from prison but was ordered to remain confined to her home. According to court documents, she was barred from leaving her apartment and her contact with family was severely restricted. In an affidavit, she described armed, camouflaged officers guarding her building.

On Thursday, more than two months after Ms. Sabga was detained, authorities released her from house arrest and revoked her detention order. On Friday, when local reporters asked Mr. Alexander about Ms. Sabga’s release, he compared her case to the search for the killer of Tupac Shakur, the American rapper.

“Tupac Shakur was shot in 1996, and the person was only charged this year,” he said, implying that the state’s investigation into Ms. Sabga would continue after her release. “It’s not over till it’s over,” he added.

The state of emergency is scheduled to expire this week, and hundreds of detainees are set to be released. Many, like Ms. Sabga and the Hadeeds, have not been charged with any crime.

item.title: Landmark Vote Held in Restive Muslim Autonomous Region in the Philippines
item.description:
Hundreds of thousands of people cast ballots on Monday in the first parliamentary election of an autonomous region in the southern Philippines, which was long a center of Muslim separatist activity and where Islamic State fighters laid siege to a city less than a decade ago.

In a sign of how restive the region remains, there were reports of violence, including a shootout that local officials said had left three people dead and more than 15 wounded near a polling station late Sunday, hours before voting began. The authorities also said they had found ballot tampering in a remote area.

The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao was established in 2019, superseding an earlier autonomous zone that was considered to have benefited only a small number of Muslim families. Monday’s election had been delayed for years over security concerns. As many as 2.3 million voters were expected to select 80 representatives, who will then pick a chief minister from among themselves.

“The polls are historic because they test the durability of the peace process, institutionalize self-rule within the constitutional framework of the Philippines, and set a precedent for democratic consolidation in a region long defined by armed struggle,” said Rommel Banlaoi, a Manila-based political and security analyst.

The region — encompassing a large section of Mindanao, the second-largest island in the Philippines, plus other smaller islands — is the only one in the country that will be governed by a parliamentary system. For decades, it was home to a separatist movement led by the Moro Islamic Liberation Front, which fought a fierce uprising that left about 120,000 people dead and pushed pockets of the region into a cycle of extreme poverty and violence.

In 2014, the group dropped its bid for full independence in return for the right to self-rule. Many fighters joined a “transitional authority” that was to be replaced eventually by the region’s own parliament. But delays in the peace process frustrated some residents. In 2017, helped by fighters from Southeast Asia and the Middle East, a local faction of the Islamic State took over the city of Marawi, leading to a five-month battle that left hundreds dead.

Yasmin Busran Lao, a 65-year-old social worker, cast her ballot at about noon on Monday at a Marawi precinct heavily guarded by the Philippine military. The city, parts of which have been rebuilt in recent years, had many checkpoints and roadblocks, she said.

“You can’t help but feel worried because when you see a lot of soldiers, they are preparing for conflict,” said Ms. Lao, whose ancestral home was laid to rubble during the 2017 siege. “I was hesitant to go out and vote.”

She noted that the region remained home to groups affiliated with the Islamic State and added, “This vote is meant for us to choose our leaders who will help rebuild.”

Farther south, the city of Cotabato, the seat of the autonomous government, was under the control of the Philippine Commission on Elections. That takeover followed the shootout and another episode, in which a suspect was injured after a homemade bomb that he was carrying prematurely exploded, said George Garcia, the commission’s chairman.

The authorities also found that some ballots had been tampered with in the remote municipality of Maluso on Basilan Island, he said.

“We determined, as of last night, ballots in 36 out of the 68 precincts had been compromised,” he told reporters in a text message, noting that the names on the ballots had already been chosen in advance.

item.title: France Mocked U.S. for Human Rights Vote, Then Quietly Apologized
item.description:
When France compared the United States to North Korea and Russia in July, the Trump administration responded by freezing the approval of a new French ambassador to Washington.

Now, after seven weeks of American pressure, France has backed down, apologizing on Friday for the social media post that set off the dispute. That will allow France’s nomination of Aurélien Lechevallier as its ambassador to Washington to move forward, according to a senior American official and a former French official with knowledge of the situation. The two spoke on the condition of anonymity, citing the delicacy of the negotiations.

The episode illustrated the strained nature of relations during the Trump era between Europe and the United States, which have diverged over the futures of Greenland, Ukraine and the postwar international order.

The dispute erupted on July 24 after the United Nations General Assembly voted 114 to 10, with 13 abstentions, to give a second four-year term to Volker Türk, an Austrian lawyer, as high commissioner of the U.N. human rights commission.

Like North Korea and Russia, the United States opposed Mr. Türk. It cited his criticism of the United States and Israel and what it said was his reluctance to condemn repressive governments in Iran and Cuba.

“The UN human rights system has been losing credibility for decades,” the United States mission to the United Nations said in a post on social media. “Volker Türk led it to its deathbed.”

Responding to that post, the French mission in Geneva posted: “The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore. Today, it stands alongside North Korea, Nicaragua, Mali & Russia, isolated. And the world no longer listens to it.” That message was reposted by the foreign ministry, which later deleted the reposting.

The State Department reacted indignantly to the post, lodging a protest with the French Embassy in Washington. At the U.N., the American delegation walked out on a French diplomat when he addressed the chamber. In Paris, the U.S. ambassador, Charles Kushner, texted President Emmanuel Macron to urge the French make a gesture to defuse the issue, according to the American official.

Mr. Kushner’s involvement as mediator was notable, given that he had himself inflamed American-French relations early in his tenure by publicly accusing France of not doing enough to combat antisemitism. He had been summoned twice to the ministry to be rebuked for interfering in France’s internal affairs, snubbing both requests.

Mr. Lechevallier, the chief of staff to the French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, had been scheduled to move to Washington this month to replace the outgoing ambassador, Laurent Bili. Like all envoys, his appointment requires approval from the host government, which American officials made clear to the French would not happen until the offending post was addressed.

Mr. Lechevallier, 50, is viewed as close to Mr. Macron, having been a classmate and adviser of his.

The State Department and the French Foreign Ministry declined to comment on the status of Mr. Lechevallier’s nomination, but both suggested that the apology would swiftly resolve the impasse.

A spokesman for the foreign ministry said, “We are committed to moving the bilateral relationship with our American partners forward.” A State Department official said, “We note and appreciate France’s statement, and look forward to working together to further shared values and interests.”

Since President Trump’s return to the White House, France’s foreign ministry has prided itself on using social media to hit back, often humorously, at the United States and other critics of Europe. It maintains a popular and sometimes snarky account on X, @FrenchResponse. In a speech last May, Mr. Barrot said the account “isn’t trolling. It’s a geopolitical tool, a real-time reframing tool.”

But this episode shows this edgy approach is not without risks, at least as far as the Trump administration is concerned. Gérard Araud, a former French ambassador to Washington, said the post complained about had crossed a line, and that France’s failure to address the situation immediately only compounded the damage.

“The French committed a mistake; they are paying the price. They should have done it earlier,” Mr. Araud said. “The U.S. has taken advantage of our ineptitude.”

item.title: Saudi Leader Meets U.S. General as Widening Conflict Threatens Oil Markets
item.description:
Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince and de facto ruler, met with the U.S. general who oversees the military’s Middle East operations on Monday as a lightning advance by Iranian-backed Houthi militants in Yemen threatened to unsettle global energy markets further.

A brief summary carried by Saudi state media said Prince Mohammed held talks with Adm. Brad Cooper, who leads the U.S. military’s Central Command, in the Saudi coastal city of Jeddah to discuss “the latest regional developments.” Central Command did not immediately comment.

Admiral Cooper began meeting with Saudi defense officials late last week to discuss intelligence sharing and munitions, according to two people familiar with his visit. They requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Diplomacy between the Trump administration and Iran on ending the war has stalled. Instead, the regional conflict that began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February has widened, with a new front opening in Yemen between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is backed by Saudi Arabia.

Last week, the Houthis, who rule much of northwestern Yemen, swept into the strategic port of Mokha on the Red Sea and also seized the island of Perim. Forces allied with the Yemeni government also withdrew from the Hunaish and Zuqar islands last week, according to Yemeni officials.

The Houthi advance has put Saudi Arabia, which has fought a long military campaign with the group, on edge.

Prince Mohammed spoke with President Trump about the escalation in Yemen last week and urged the United States to take military action against the Houthis, according to officials with knowledge of the conversations. Mr. Trump told him he was not willing to do so, the officials said.

The territorial gains have given the militants greater sway over the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a maritime choke point in the Red Sea.

Houthi officials have vowed to block Saudi shipping in the waterway, threatening another critical route for global oil shipments. Iran has effectively blockaded the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf since the U.S.-Israeli attack in late February, causing energy prices to soar.

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, jumped nearly 4 percent to over $108 a barrel, on Monday, reflecting investor worries over continued instability in the Middle East. The price of Brent is roughly 50 percent higher than before the war.

The renewed fighting has effectively reignited the Yemeni civil war, which had been largely quiet since a 2022 cease-fire. Saudi-aligned forces have attacked Houthi territory, while Houthi forces have repeatedly fired at sites in Saudi Arabia that they say are military and energy installations.

On Monday, the Saudi government’s civil defense issued alerts for the southern cities of Khamis Mushait and Abha, warning of incoming attacks. There were no reports of casualties.

item.title: China’s Top Spy Chief Warns A.I. Is a Threat to Party Rule
item.description:
China’s top spy chief has warned that artificial intelligence could pose a direct threat to the Chinese Communist Party’s hold on power, in what is the highest-level and most detailed articulation yet of how Beijing sees the technology’s security risks.

The unusually blunt assessment by Chen Yixin, the head of China’s Ministry of State Security, is in contrast to the warnings dominating the A.I. debate in the United States, which have focused on the possibility that A.I. could slip out of human control or pose a threat to humanity itself.

In an article published on Sunday in the state-run magazine China Cyberspace, Mr. Chen called for more party control over A.I. and stricter government oversight. This, he said, was necessary to protect political stability at home; to defend against increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks and misinformation campaigns from “hostile forces”; and to compete militarily with countries like the United States.

Mr. Chen referred specifically to U.S. tech companies and their A.I. models — like Claude Mythos and GPT-5.5-Cyber — as examples of new threats to cybersecurity. He also described the danger that foreign intelligence agencies might use A.I. for “large-scale espionage” and attacks on China’s critical infrastructure.

The warning from the powerful security agency makes clear that China sees foreign A.I. models as an active threat to China, according to Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University. That effectively draws a red line before talks between American and Chinese officials on A.I. safety risks, expected ahead of a meeting between President Trump and China’s leader, Xi Jinping, on Sept. 24 in Washington.

“Beijing is going into these talks viewing A.I. safety not as a shared humanitarian mission, but through an adversarial lens,” Mr. Gao said. It is making clear to Chinese tech firms and foreign rivals that “data sovereignty and political security will never be traded away for international safety accords,” he added.

Mr. Chen’s remarks are not the first time the security agency has spoken about the dangers of A.I., but they are the most comprehensive and signal Beijing’s growing concern about the industry. The security chief outlined several ways that A.I. could pose a threat to China:

Undermining the security of the Communist Party. The government’s top priority has long been maintaining the power of the ruling party. Mr. Chen’s article warns that those with “ulterior motives” could use A.I. to generate fake videos and audio to wage a “propaganda war” against China.

“They’re worried, among other things, of say a deepfake of a Chinese official saying something that wasn’t actually said, and that spreading rapidly and destabilizing everything,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution who studies Chinese technology and industrial policy. “Someone thinks that Xi Jinping made some announcement which he didn’t actually. That could sow chaos.”

Attacks on China’s critical infrastructure. Mr. Chen, the spy chief, wrote that the technical and financial barriers to launching cyberattacks had been drastically lowered because of A.I. This, he said, posed “serious risks” to China’s information infrastructure. Last week, a small team of researchers in California demonstrated that risk when they disclosed a hacking tool that could take control of millions of users’ accounts on WeChat, China’s most widely used messaging app.

Leaks of sensitive information. Chinese users using foreign models could cause large-scale data leaks, the article noted. Anthropic, the company behind Claude and other A.I. models, said last week that the Chinese start-up Moonshot AI had routed queries by its users to Claude. Those queries included sensitive data, including video surveillance linked to the Chinese military, as well as proprietary information from high-profile Chinese technology companies.

More intense military competition. The U.S. military’s use of A.I. in the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran was an example of how warfare has been “fundamentally transformed,” Mr. Chen wrote. He says that whoever can harness the power of tools such as algorithms to achieve more precise sensing and targeting, “will gain the initiative on the battlefield.”

The warning adds to a growing drumbeat of concern from Chinese officials about the risks of A.I. Under Mr. Xi, China has deemed A.I. a strategic technology that is critical to the country’s development and ability to compete with the United States. At the same time, officials have begun to issue warnings and new guidelines for regulating the industry.

Previous warnings from Chinese regulators have tended to focus on specific issues, such as when the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said in July that it had detected a security risk in some versions of Anthropic’s coding tool, Claude Code. Regulators have also repeatedly warned domestic users about the risks of A.I. assistants like OpenClaw.

“This is now a much more broad-based sort of warning, not about a specific threat from this one model or this one vulnerability, but a broader paradigm shift in how A.I. will create new risk for China,” said Mr. Chan of Brookings.

“It’s about taking these new powerful tools seriously and realizing there are a lot of vulnerabilities and China needs to move faster, and also use A.I. to patch those vulnerabilities, and defend against these new powerful cyber-actors,” he said.

Even as China’s security chief was articulating the country’s concerns about A.I., its Foreign Ministry was accusing U.S. companies of hyping the dangers of the technology.

That was in response to calls by some Western A.I. executives like Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, for Washington to clamp down on Chinese companies.

In an open letter over the weekend, Mr. Amodei said that democracies must keep their lead over China. He backed restrictions on selling powerful A.I. chips to the country, among other measures to slow China’s progress enough to widen America’s lead.

Asked if China’s A.I. industry posed a threat to the United States, Guo Jiakun, a spokesman for China’s Foreign Ministry, said on Monday that such “threat narratives” and “malicious competition” would only make it harder for countries to work together on the regulation of A.I.

In an editorial on Sunday, the Communist Party-run tabloid, the Global Times, said that China played a central role as one of the world’s main suppliers of A.I. tools. It described Mr. Amodei’s call for the United States to contain China’s development as an “unrealistic delusion.”

item.title: The New Moscow: A Digital Utopia Doubling as a Surveillance Trap
item.description:
On the surface, today’s Moscow is a technological wonderland. You can use your face to pay for almost anything, like subway fares, or even to finalize the purchase of an apartment. Robots scurry across sidewalks making 15-minute grocery deliveries, and driverless taxis are set to begin commercial service this year.

Underpinning many of the modern amenities is a robust digital infrastructure developed by the city government that has made life not only easier, but also safer. Policing aided by digital tools has helped cement Moscow’s transformation from the raw, unforgiving place it was 25 years ago, plagued by home burglaries, street muggings and murders.

But there is a cost to the convenience and security: an expanding surveillance state.

Moscow’s roughly 300,000 CCTV cameras make it one of the most heavily watched cities in the world. It is impossible to avoid a lens while simply walking through the city. The same cameras that whisk subway passengers through turnstiles are also used to monitor and flag people.

In April, a Russian rock musician was detained by the police at a railway terminal in St. Petersburg after surveillance cameras mistook him for a similar-looking Ukrainian public figure wanted by the state. After checking his face and pulling at his hair to ensure it was not a wig, they let him go.

The CCTV network is linked to biometric databases. Submission of biometric data is voluntary in Russia, but it is encouraged in widespread advertisements, and citizens cannot take full advantage of digital services without complying.

These databases help the authorities target political dissent in addition to crime. Biometric feeds can be used to hunt down critics of the government after they hold gatherings. The days when outspoken Russians could flee to remote towns to avoid the authorities, as they did during Stalin’s purges, are largely over.

As of July, around 10 million Russians were using biometrics-driven applications in some form, and the Kremlin wants to increase that number, pushing citizens to adopt the tools for identification not only at train stations, but also at airports. This year, Moscow City Hall announced that a biometric system would recognize passengers on buses and trams, automatically deducting their fare once they confirmed the transaction in an app.

Other major European cities also have large CCTV networks, most notably London. Moscow’s, however, is more centralized and uses biometrics to identify people spotted by cameras with fewer restrictions.

With Russia’s war in Ukraine, the stakes behind the growing surveillance have become higher.

Rumors of a new wave of military conscription, the first major mobilization since the early months of the war, have swept through Russia. While in the recent past it was relatively simple to evade a draft because enlistment offices were buried under paper files, artificial intelligence-enhanced digitized systems make that almost impossible now. The authorities introduced electronic summonses that carry the full legal weight of paper notices after thousands of Russians fled the draft in 2022.

In March, Vlad, 28, an art and fashion photographer, received a summons to appear at a military enlistment office for a mandatory medical examination. Through the State Services app — a centralized portal for government services, medical care and identity verification — he learned that he had been barred from leaving the country until he complied.

Vlad, who asked that his last name be withheld for fear of repercussions, said he now lived “in fear” as he defied the summons, which he believes could be a prelude to being sent off to war.

“There is total control because you give up so much data that your every step can be traced,” he said. He has stopped using the subway, terrified of the cameras.

Kremlin-aligned analysts argue that the government is using convenient apps and data collection to build a system that is more responsive to people’s needs than what can be provided by Western democracies, which struggle to plan long term because of changes in government and, in some cases, limit digital services because of privacy concerns.

Russia remains steps away from China’s “social credit” system, which rates people on their behavior in financial, legal and other matters and limits the freedom of offenders. But Russian technocrats clearly view Beijing’s digital architecture as a blueprint.

Gleb Kuznetsov, a political analyst who previously worked for a major Kremlin-aligned think tank, pointed to Moscow under its longtime mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, and to Shenzhen, the Chinese high-tech megacity, as urban models superior to Western capitals.

“Sobyanin’s approval rating is high not because ‘the elections lack competition,’” Mr. Kuznetsov said in response to written questions, “but because the city government genuinely works in the interest of its residents.”

The Russian authorities, however, can be quick to pull the plug on the networks undergirding these digital amenities when they perceive a security threat, highlighting a tension between technocratic agencies and the security services.

In March, for instance, mobile internet services were abruptly shut down for more than two weeks across much of central Moscow, including in the subway system, temporarily rendering many of the city’s prized digital services useless.

Residents were left stunned by the blackout, which some analysts speculated was a result of intense state paranoia after the assassination of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Iran.

“Russia is going to go back to a situation 25 years ago where you have ‘patchwork globalization,’” said Jeremy Morris, an ethnologist who is one of the few Western academics who continue to conduct fieldwork in Russia.

“You could go into one place and it would be super, super cybernetic and technological,” he added, “and then you walk out of the zone of coverage and you’re back to a basic economy.”

According to a Russian official involved in developing digital infrastructure, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak publicly, a quiet war is being waged within the state.

Technocratic agencies like the Ministry of Digital Development, he said, are colliding with the Federal Security Service, or F.S.B. — specifically its notorious political-policing department. While it has access to digital tools, the F.S.B. was not involved in creating them. It favors old-school analog methods of monitoring and controlling society, the official said, even if that means breaking the technology that the technocrats spent billions building.

The F.S.B.’s stance is partly driven by institutional self-preservation, as A.I. threatens to erode the justification for its sprawling apparatus of human agents, the official said.

Ultimately, both the digital and security agencies are competing for the ear and mind of one man: President Vladimir V. Putin, who has demanded that the government develop A.I. while insulating it from Western influence.

In April, speaking at a high-profile Kremlin meeting on A.I., Mr. Putin framed the stakes in existential terms. “The sovereignty of the Russian state in the near future — and, without exaggeration, its very existence — depends on our ability to perform well in A.I., along with digital platforms and autonomous systems,” he said.

Yet for all of its ambitions, Russia lacks the infrastructure and hardware to develop the technology in isolation from China and the United States. Western sanctions related to the invasion of Ukraine have limited Russia’s access to cutting-edge chips, and many of its top technical minds have left the country since the war began in 2022.

Russia’s two flagship A.I. models — one developed by the country’s largest state-owned bank and the other by its leading domestic tech company — were “inspired” by or heavily rely on Chinese open-source architectures.

In the end, said Ilya Grashchenkov, a Moscow-based political analyst, Russia is likely to be defined by what he called an attempt to “combine the seemingly incompatible.” That, he said, involves building an “external digital perimeter” to close the country off from the world, while accelerating digitization within Russia.

Vlad, the photographer who received the military summons, said he would gladly do away with the frictionless, high-tech conveniences if it meant getting back the freedom that was truly missing.

Life in Russia, he said, now resembles “living in an oxygen mask.”

Every time I come to Moscow, I am amazed by how convenient and seamless digital services have become in the city. But the flip side of that comfort is that you cannot do anything — use public transportation or make a simple purchase — without leaving a digital trace.

The Russian government is aggressively using biometrics and A.I. to make life more modern on the one hand, but to exercise strict control over every aspect of daily life on the other. There is also a quiet competition within the state between younger, tech-savvy technocratic agencies and KGB-style security services, who prefer traditional tools and need to justify their massive headcount.

While this reads like a story specific to Russia, it also mirrors a broader global trend. As governments everywhere begin using A.I. to enforce compliance universally and frictionlessly, the fundamental relationship between society and the state is bound to change.

item.title: Russian Strike on Train Station Near Poland Seen as Warning to Kyiv’s Allies
item.description:
Ukraine’s rail network is a link to the West. With airspace over the country closed, its trains crawl toward the border day and night, ferrying officials and dignitaries, along with ordinary people, to and from the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv. The railway is a lifeline, and a potent symbol of support.

European officials say that Russia’s weekend strike on a station near the Ukraine-Poland border, which hit perilously close to departing foreign visitors including the former C.I.A. director David Petraeus, was an attack not just on Ukrainian infrastructure, but on those ties.

It was not immediately clear whether Moscow intended to target any particular official. Attacks on railways are common, and the Russian Defense Ministry said that the military was taking aim at routes “used to transport military cargo,” according to the Russian news agency TASS.

But European leaders said the incident was part of an escalating Russian campaign to create confusion and to weaken the Western alliance at a particularly dangerous moment for Ukraine.

“It is clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine, from going to Ukraine to show support,” Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, said on Monday. “The question for us is, ‘What do we take from that message?’”

Governments and researchers have accused Russia in recent years of sabotage and of hybrid attacks aimed at Ukraine’s allies. A drone containing an explosive device was found in the freight terminal of an airport in Leipzig, eastern Germany, last month, an incident that Berlin blamed Moscow for. Misinformation and election interference by Russia have become common. So has GPS jamming, which can disrupt communication and navigation.

Josh Holder/The New York Times

The timing of the attack was notable. The drone strike hit a train close to one ridden by Mr. Petraeus and came shortly after the departure of another, carrying the former British prime minister Boris Johnson and other European politicians and diplomats.

The NATO secretary general, Mark Rutte, said the strike showed “desperation” on the part of President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia. NATO would respond, Mr. Rutte said, by doubling down on support for Ukraine and with potential covert action.

Philip Bednarczyk, the Warsaw office director at the German Marshall Fund, a think tank, said that Russia’s attacks served to test “over and over again” whether NATO allies were committed to defending one another.

Mr. Bednarczyk pointed out that while incidents so far had been isolated, many in Poland were bracing for further escalation this winter, perhaps even into something coordinated. Mr. Bednarczyk said that he already knew friends who had begun to avoid taking the train into Kyiv from Warsaw, opting to drive instead.

“It’s an important artery,” he said of the rail link to Poland.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk of Poland said that Russia’s escalation was “becoming a reality” and that he would review plans to protect his country’s railways and industries.

He added that the most recent strikes showed that Russia was more willing than ever to deploy longer-range, high-precision, jet-powered drones to threaten NATO.

“We do not want to give in to nervousness — emotions are the last thing needed here,” Mr. Tusk said. “But there is no doubt that we, together with our allies, must be prepared for a joint response should the need arise.”

Russia’s latest strike comes at a moment when European nations are considering how they can best support Ukraine as the war becomes ever more costly and the fighting shows no sign of ending soon.

The European Union finalized a support package of 90 billion euros, about $100 billion, for Ukraine this year. But Kyiv’s financial needs are growing under a barrage of Russian attacks, reviving a conversation among European nations about how to continue the financial backing.

Some countries are again contemplating whether it might make sense to use Russian sovereign assets frozen in Europe to support Ukraine — an idea that was considered last year, but ultimately rejected.

Petteri Orpo, the prime minister of Finland, said on Monday that the train station attack was an attempt to break European unity, adding that Moscow was wrong to think such efforts would succeed.

“This is a very dangerous game they are playing now,” Mr. Orpo noted.

Anatol Magdziarz contributed reporting.
